summary: Weekly pilot sync focused on throughput regression observed over last 48h. Investigated 'batch drift' where average batch sizes dropped because of prompt-length variance and KV-cache thrash causing higher per-token compute. Agreed on soak test and queue/backpressure playbook changes; AE to follow up on Dedicated burst pricing. Canonical next steps recorded.
topics:
1) Recent latency/throughput regression overview
2) Continuous batching behavior + prompt length distributions
3) KV cache eviction patterns and warmup effects
4) Concurrency targets & autoscale policy tweaks
5) Playbook: backpressure thresholds and fallback model routing
6) Next steps and responsibilities
transcript:
[00:00] Evan Rhodes: Okay everyone thanks for joining, we've got 55 minutes on the docket, quick agenda. Clara will share the perf findings and then we can dig into tuning.
[00:12] Clara Nguyen: Yeah hi, hey, so pulling up the dashboard — the big thing we saw over the weekend was what I'm calling batch drift, so the continuous-batcher is still batching but the average batch size slid from 18 to about 8 on peak, which raised latency.
[00:25] Sofia Morales: Wait when you say batch drift, is that because of a change in traffic or did our prompt templates change? We didn't release anything.
[00:33] Clara Nguyen: Good question. We checked release tags, nothing. It correlates to an uptick in short, extremely short prompts — like one or two tokens for health-check style calls — that were interleaving with longer completions. The batcher heuristics currently flush earlier when max-wait is hit so those shorts reduce batch occupancy.
[00:52] Ben Chu: Another factor we saw in infra traces is KV cache eviction — there were a couple full-GPU memory pressure events that evicted cold cache and that caused first-token latency spikes — which then kicked request routing to fallback model for a small percent.
[01:05] Rajesh Iyer: Does the fallback model add extra latency or is it cheaper? We don't want quality regressions.
[01:10] Clara Nguyen: Fallbacks are generally smaller model variants — they respond faster per-token in steady state for short requests but produce different output qualities. The issue is the extra routing and warmup adds a couple 100 ms on p95 in the timeframe we observed.
[01:23] Evan Rhodes: Right, and from a throughput POV the combined effect of lower batch occupancy plus transient warmup means your throughput dropped ~22% at peak. We pulled numbers from Thursday night and you can see the correlation to spikes in short prompt ratio.
[01:37] Tara Lim: We also saw retries from our client side during those tail spikes, which inflated requests and made the situation worse.
[01:43] Clara Nguyen: Exactly, retry amplification is classic. So the playbook options we discussed — and I want to frame them — are: 1) adjust batcher max-wait and prefer occupancy heuristics; 2) implement client-side jitter + better retry windows; 3) kv-cache sizing/tuning or pinning hot prefix; 4) conservative autoscale/burst capacity during peak windows.
[02:05] Sofia Morales: If we change max-wait won't that increase p50 for short requests? Our UX team wants snappy feedback for small requests.
[02:12] Clara Nguyen: There's a tradeoff, yes. One hybrid approach is dynamic max-wait based on recent short-prompt fraction — when fraction goes up reduce preference for occupancy for N seconds. That keeps snappy small requests but stabilizes batch sizes during mixed traffic.
[02:26] Ben Chu: On the KV side, can Redwood pin embeddings or prefixes in memory? We have a handful of hot prefixes which are high hit-rate.
[02:31] Clara Nguyen: We can recommend warmup hints and suggest prefix pinning in Dedicated/private deployments — and we can tune eviction thresholds. For hosted we can surface hints — but pinning requires dedicated allocation.
[02:40] Rajesh Iyer: We're evaluating Dedicated for guaranteed burst capacity — can you share 3-month pilot pricing?
[02:46] Evan Rhodes: Yep I'll send a short invoice and pricing spreadsheet after the call. We'll include a burst slab for peak hours.
[02:52] [03:00] Clara Nguyen: I want to call out a small anomaly — the continuous-batching algorithm currently uses observed sequence-length buckets; when the short-prompt percent crosses 35% the effective batch size collapses. That threshold looked tuned for more homogeneous traffic; for mixed workloads we recommend tuning to 50% or implementing an occupancy bias factor.
[03:18] Sofia Morales: Could we add a client header to mark health-checks so the batcher ignores them from mixing?
[03:22] Clara Nguyen: Absolutely, a small header like X-Intent: probe can be used to tag and optionally route to a low-latency pool or to deprioritize batching interference. That's a low-effort fix on the client side.
[03:30] Ben Chu: About the soak — what are we running? Concurrency target and duration?
[03:33] Clara Nguyen: Proposed: 30 minutes at 120 concurrency with the live prompt mix (we'll replay an anonymized sample you provide). Capture p50/p95/p99 and batch-size distribution every 60s.
[03:42] Rajesh Iyer: 120 is higher than our expected steady concurrency — why that number?
[03:45] Clara Nguyen: It's a margin above your observed peak (95th) to validate autoscale and burst handling. If the soak passes we can lower conservative safety limits.
[03:52] Evan Rhodes: Also want to discuss backpressure thresholds — right now the queue depth hard cap is 200 and we observed transient queueing to 170; recommended playbook is soft backpressure at 120 and hard reject at 220 with exponential retry hints returned to client. This avoids large queues that cause eviction/warmup churn.
[04:12] Tara Lim: Who owns changing these thresholds in staging?
[04:14] Ben Chu: Infra will push staging changes once Redwood provides recommended values and a rollback plan.
[04:20] Clara Nguyen: I'll write up the threshold doc and include simulation notes — how queue growth maps to batch occupancy and latency.
[04:28] Sofia Morales: Can you also simulate a scenario with 40% short prompts so we can see worst-case?
[04:33] Clara Nguyen: Yep we'll include that in the soak matrix.
[04:36] Evan Rhodes: For the canary timeline — proposed for March 2: modify autoscale to more aggressive burst allow for 90 minutes in staging then monitor. Rajesh, confirm your windows.
[04:47] Rajesh Iyer: I'll confirm with ops and get back by Feb 9.
[04:50] [05:00] Quick recaps, broken items and who does what.
[05:06] Evan Rhodes: Anything else on security/compliance? Last time Rajesh mentioned SOC2.
[05:11] Rajesh Iyer: We're good but will need the audit logs for the pilot period, retention settings.
[05:16] Evan Rhodes: We'll surface the audit-log retention options in the follow-up email.
[05:20] Clara Nguyen: One last note — we noticed a tiny subset of requests were routed cross-region during capacity spikes; might be worth pinning region routing during the pilot to reduce variability.
[05:29] Ben Chu: Agreed.
[05:32] Evan Rhodes: Great — I'll send notes, pricing, and next actions today. Clara will run the soak and deliver graphs. Thanks everyone.
[05:41] Meeting ends
